overview: The imported Spanish Guinea outline covers mainland Río Muni, not the whole island-and-mainland colony. In the late nineteenth century Spanish claims greatly exceeded effective control. The 1900 Treaty of Paris recognized a mainland territory, but much of its interior remained outside colonial occupation into the twentieth century.

periods.title: Claims and coastal footholds
periods.summary: Spanish presence was limited while European powers competed for territory.

periods.title: A border before full occupation
periods.summary: The treaty defined claims; expansion into the interior continued.

items.text: The 1900 settlement between France and Spain did not make everyone within the new border Spanish subjects under effective daily administration overnight. Spanish presence remained coastal, and occupation of the interior continued into the 1920s. The colored outline gets ahead of control on the ground.

A 1902 order treated European people and African converts to Christianity under the Spanish penal code, while directing other African cases toward local custom and general legal principles. Religious classification helped determine legal treatment: colonial courts were not a system of equal citizenship.

Colonial officials made local chiefs responsible for maintaining villages, receiving European travelers and pursuing fugitives. Chiefs also supplied workers for public projects and plantations. These duties could turn an existing community office into an instrument of coercion, although chiefs sometimes protested the demands imposed on their people.

A Fang plate from the Bata district shows how a meal could begin with basketry. Collected in the 1880s, it is woven from melongo fibre and measures about 24.5 centimetres across. The museum explains that diners placed leaves over this kind of plate before eating.

The same type of woven plate could work as a hand-turned support for making pottery. Men made these plates; women also used them for ceramic work, according to the museum. A useful object could have two careers: dinner service and pottery workshop.

Preparing melongo for basketry meant cutting, peeling and drying the plant material, then splitting it into strips of suitable thickness. The catalogue connects that skill to baskets, plates and crab traps. Changing the weave could change a bundle of fibre into a household tool or a way to catch supper.

A Balengue comb collected during the 1884 to 1886 expedition has 27 bamboo teeth held together by woven plant fibre. It is less than nine centimetres tall. The object brings history down to a familiar scale: somebody had to deal with their hair before starting the day.

The comb catalogue also describes Fang women and men oiling their hair with palm oil before combing, with the intention of avoiding lice. This is evidence of a recorded grooming practice and its purpose, not a modern test of how well it prevented parasites.

Ossorio’s collection includes a nineteenth-century tool from the Río Congüe catalogued as a carpenter’s plane. Alongside the decorated household objects, it preserves evidence of skilled woodworking. The museum record names the locality and collector, but leaves the individual craftsperson anonymous.

sections.title: Learning, language and a later ending

items.text: Bata had a complicated school history: French Spiritan missionaries taught in Spanish and remained there until 1919. From the 1910s, rural teaching expanded through African catechists and colonial-guard interpreters. Schooling trained clerks and other assistants while also pressing children toward Spanish language and colonial loyalties.

Elsewhere in the same colony, on Bioko rather than this mainland outline, Banapá’s school taught printing, shoemaking, tailoring, carpentry and masonry. Its press produced La Guinea Española from 1903. The biography of pupil Joaquín Sialo records workshops, a band and an experimental farm: education involved tools as well as books.

A short Fang language sample in the museum’s present-day spelling is “along ncueng”, translated as “make a basket.” It accompanies the nineteenth-century woven plate in the catalogue. These Latin letters record spoken Fang; the phrase is a modern explanatory transcription, not writing discovered on the plate.

For period writing, a Spanish military map published in 1900 bears the catalogued title “Mapa de la Guinea Española”: “Map of Spanish Guinea.” Its main scale is 1:500,000, with a much more detailed Río Muni inset. Survey information helped officials turn claims into lines on paper.
Equatorial Guinea gained independence on 12 October 1968. Spanish colonial rule ended decades after this map label stops.

ending.text: Spanish rule continued beyond the 1914 map cutoff. Equatorial Guinea became independent on 12 October 1968; mainland communities continued within the new state.
